title: The Importance of Being Earnest — Act I opening
source: Oscar Wilde, The Importance of Being Earnest (1895). Public domain.

lines.text: Did you hear what I was playing, Lane?
I didn't think it polite to listen, sir.
I'm sorry for that, for your sake. I don't play accurately.
lines.paraphrase: I'm sorry about that, for your benefit. I don't play very precisely.

lines.text: Anyone can play accurately, but I play with wonderful expression.
lines.paraphrase: Anyone can play correctly, though my playing has marvellous expression.

lines.text: As far as the piano is concerned, sentiment is my forte. I keep science for Life.
lines.paraphrase: When it comes to the piano, feeling is my strength. Science I save for real life.

lines.text: And, speaking of the science of Life, have you got the cucumber sandwiches cut for Lady Bracknell?
lines.paraphrase: Speaking of science and life, did you get the cucumber sandwiches ready for Lady Bracknell?

lines.text: Oh! by the way, Lane, I see from your book that on Thursday night, when Lord Shoreman and Mr. Worthing were dining with me, eight bottles of champagne are entered as having been consumed.
lines.paraphrase: By the way, Lane, your book says that on Thursday, when Lord Shoreman and Mr. Worthing dined here, eight bottles of champagne got drunk.

lines.text: Yes, sir; eight bottles and a pint.
Why is it that at a bachelor's establishment the servants invariably drink the champagne? I ask merely for information.
I attribute it to the superior quality of the wine, sir. I have often observed that in married households the champagne is rarely of a first-rate brand.
lines.paraphrase: I put it down to how good the wine is, sir. In married homes, I find, the champagne is seldom first-rate.

lines.text: Good heavens! Is marriage so demoralising as that?
I believe it is a very pleasant state, sir. I have had very little experience of it myself up to the present.
lines.paraphrase: I hear it is a pleasant state to be in, sir. I have not had much experience of it myself so far.
